subject: chemistry

items.q: Which statement describes a metallic bond?
items.correct: The electrostatic attraction between a lattice of cations and delocalized electrons
items.misconception: The sharing of electron pairs between each metal atom and its nearest neighbours
items.why: Bonds are first met as lines between pairs of atoms in covalent molecules, and diagrams of metal lattices show atoms touching their neighbours, which invites a bond along each line of contact. Counting bonds from the group number feels like the valency rule used for molecules. Ball-and-stick and spring models present bonds as physical links that can flex, so a change of shape is pictured as bonds bending. In a metal the valence electrons are delocalized over the whole lattice, not shared in pairs between two atoms. The bonding is the electrostatic attraction between the lattice of cations and these electrons; it has no fixed direction, which is why layers of cations can slide without the bonding being broken.
items.specStatementText: A metallic bond is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of cations and delocalized electrons.
items.random_wrong: The attraction between cations and anions formed by electron transfer between metal atoms

items.q: Which statement about a piece of solid sodium is correct?
items.correct: It is neutral, with one delocalized electron for each Na⁺ ion in its lattice.
items.misconception: It carries a positive charge, because its atoms have lost their outer electrons.
items.why: The words used for ionic bonding ('the metal atom loses its outer electrons') are reused for metals. In ionic bonding the electrons really do leave the metal atom for another atom, so 'loses' suggests the electrons have gone, and the cations are pictured with nothing to balance them. Metal atoms release their valence electrons into a delocalized system that belongs to the whole lattice; the electrons remain in the metal. Solid sodium has one delocalized electron for each Na⁺ ion and solid magnesium two for each Mg²⁺ ion, so the metal is neutral.
items.specStatementText: A metallic bond is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of cations and delocalized electrons.
items.random_wrong: It contains no ions; its lattice is made only of neutral sodium atoms.

items.q: Copper is used for the wires in household electrical cables because it conducts electricity very well. What carries the electric current through a copper wire?
items.correct: The copper's delocalized electrons, drifting through the lattice
items.misconception: Copper cations, moving through the lattice towards the negative terminal
items.why: Conduction by moving ions is taught for molten and aqueous ionic compounds, and the word 'ion' also appears in the metallic model, so the mechanism is transferred. The rule 'charged particles must be free to move' is right, but the particles are wrongly identified. Mobile ions carry the current in electrolytes. In a solid metal the cations are held in the lattice, and a metal wire does not change in composition when it conducts. The mobile charge carriers are the delocalized electrons.
items.specStatementText: A metallic bond is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of cations and delocalized electrons.
items.random_wrong: Electrons from the power supply; the copper's own electrons stay in place

items.q: Aluminium is used for heat sinks, which carry thermal energy away from computer processors. Which statement explains why aluminium is suitable?
items.correct: Its delocalized electrons carry kinetic energy rapidly through the whole metal.
items.misconception: Its high melting point lets it absorb all the heat without melting.
items.why: 'Withstanding heat' is the obvious everyday requirement of anything that gets hot, and 'high melting point' is a frequent answer in examinations on why metals are used for cooking pans; students do not separate surviving a temperature from transferring energy. Surviving a temperature and transferring energy are different properties. A heat sink works by conducting energy rapidly away from a hot component, which metals do through their delocalized electrons; its melting point is far above the temperatures it meets and is not the reason for the choice.
items.specStatementText: A metallic bond is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of cations and delocalized electrons.
items.random_wrong: Its vibrating ions pass the energy on; its electrons play no part.

items.q: Aluminium is rolled into kitchen foil less than 0.02 mm thick without cracking. Which statement explains this property of aluminium?
items.correct: Its layers of cations slide, staying attracted to the delocalized electrons around them.
items.misconception: Its metallic bonds are weak, so the rollers can easily push its atoms apart.
items.why: In everyday language 'easily bent' suggests 'weak'. Students link a change of shape with bonds breaking and so read malleability as a sign of weak bonding, although many easily shaped metals, such as copper (1085 °C) and gold (1064 °C), melt above 1000 °C. Malleability depends on the direction-free nature of metallic bonding, not on its weakness. When layers of cations slide, the attraction between the cations and the delocalized electrons is maintained, so the metal changes shape without the bonding being broken.
items.specStatementText: A metallic bond is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of cations and delocalized electrons.
items.random_wrong: Its bonds between neighbouring atoms bend like hinges instead of breaking.

items.q: The melting points of three period 3 metals are sodium 97.8 °C, magnesium 650 °C and aluminium 660 °C. Which statement explains why the melting point increases from sodium to aluminium?
items.correct: The cations have a higher charge and a smaller radius, so the metallic bonding is stronger.
items.misconception: The relative atomic mass rises, so the heavier atoms need more energy to separate.
items.why: Heavier objects are harder to move in everyday experience, and for simple molecular substances boiling points often do rise with molar mass (through stronger London forces), so mass becomes a general-purpose explanation of melting and boiling points. In a metal, melting depends on the attraction between the cations and the delocalized electrons. This attraction is set by the charge on the cations and their radius (the electron density), and it can fall while mass rises, as it does down group 1.
items.specStatementText: The strength of a metallic bond depends on the charge of the ions and the radius of the metal ion.
items.random_wrong: Each atom forms more covalent bonds to its neighbours: one for Na, two for Mg and three for Al.

items.q: The melting points of the group 1 metals decrease down the group: lithium 180.5 °C, sodium 97.8 °C, potassium 63.5 °C. Which statement explains this trend?
items.correct: The cation radius increases, so the delocalized electrons are attracted less strongly.
items.misconception: Reactivity increases down the group, so the bonds break more easily when the metal is heated.
items.why: Group 1 trends are learned side by side ('down the group reactivity increases and melting point decreases'), and students treat one trend as the cause of the other. Reactivity concerns how readily a metal atom loses electrons in a reaction with another substance; melting point concerns the strength of the attraction between cations and delocalized electrons in the metal itself. They can be correlated within a group without one explaining the other.
items.specStatementText: The strength of a metallic bond depends on the charge of the ions and the radius of the metal ion.
items.random_wrong: Larger atoms form longer and weaker covalent bonds with each of their neighbouring atoms.

items.q: Data for three metals are shown as (A_r; cation; cation radius; melting point): lithium (6.94; Li⁺; 76 pm; 180.5 °C), sodium (22.99; Na⁺; 102 pm; 97.8 °C), calcium (40.08; Ca²⁺; 100 pm; 842 °C). Which statement explains these data using the metallic model?
items.correct: Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ are almost the same size, so the higher charge of Ca²⁺ gives calcium much stronger bonding.
items.misconception: Cation radius decides bond strength: the smallest ion, Li⁺, should give the strongest bonding.
items.why: The group 1 trend, where the charge stays +1 and only the radius changes, is usually the first and most practised example, so 'smaller ion, stronger bond' is learned as the whole rule. A cation of higher charge contributes more delocalized electrons and attracts them more strongly, so charge and radius must both be considered. Compare metals whose cations differ in only one of these factors to see the effect of each.
items.specStatementText: The strength of a metallic bond depends on the charge of the ions and the radius of the metal ion.
items.random_wrong: Melting point rises with A_r: calcium has the heaviest atoms and the highest melting point.

items.q: Calcium ([Ar] 4s²) melts at 842 °C. Titanium ([Ar] 3d² 4s²), the next metal but one in period 4, melts at 1668 °C. Which statement explains the higher melting point of titanium?
items.correct: Its 3d as well as its 4s electrons are delocalized, so the electron density is higher.
items.misconception: Its extra 3d electrons give stronger London forces between its atoms than calcium's have.
items.why: Melting and boiling are often taught first for simple molecular substances, where they overcome intermolecular forces that increase with the number of electrons. 'Melting overcomes intermolecular forces' is then applied to every substance, including giant metallic structures. A metal has no molecules and no intermolecular forces in the sense used for molecular substances. It is a giant structure held by metallic bonding, whose strength depends on the charge and radius of the cations, not on the total number of electrons in each atom.
items.random_wrong: Its atoms are heavier than calcium atoms, so more energy is needed to separate them.

items.q: Iron ([Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²) is a transition element. Which statement explains the electrical conductivity of solid iron?
items.correct: Its 3d and 4s electrons are delocalized and drift when a potential difference is applied.
items.misconception: Its 4s electrons are delocalized, but its 3d electrons are core electrons fixed on the cations.
items.why: The 4s sublevel fills before 3d and is the one from which electrons are first lost when transition elements form ions, so students treat 4s as the only outer (valence) level and the 3d electrons as part of the core. The 3d and 4s sublevels of a transition element are close in energy, so the 3d electrons are valence electrons, not core electrons. In the metallic lattice they are delocalized along with the 4s electrons, which is why transition elements have much higher melting points than the s-block metals of the same period.
items.random_wrong: Its cations move through the lattice towards the negative terminal, carrying the charge.

items.q: Are the particles in the lattice of a solid metal atoms or ions?
items.correct: Ions. In the metallic model each metal atom has released its valence electrons into a delocalized system, so the lattice consists of cations surrounded by delocalized electrons.
items.misconception: A metal is made of neutral metal atoms; ions exist only in compounds such as salts.
items.why: Elements are introduced as 'made of one type of atom', and ions are first met in ionic compounds of metals with non-metals, so students reserve the word 'ion' for compounds and picture a lump of metal as a stack of intact atoms. In a metal each atom contributes its valence electrons to a delocalized system shared by the whole lattice, leaving a cation (Na⁺ in sodium, Mg²⁺ in magnesium). The metal is still an element, because all the cations are of one element, and the sample is neutral overall because the delocalized electrons balance their charge.
items.specStatementText: A metallic bond is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of cations and delocalized electrons.

items.q: Do the delocalized electrons take part in conduction through a metal?
items.correct: Yes. The delocalized electrons carry the electric current, and they also carry most of the thermal energy: they gain kinetic energy in the hot region and move rapidly through the lattice. Vibrations of the cations contribute to thermal conduction too, but far less.
items.misconception: Conduction through a solid, including a metal, is the passing of energy from one vibrating particle to the next; the delocalized electrons take no part.
items.why: Conduction in solids is taught with the particle model: particles vibrate more when heated and pass the vibration to their neighbours. This picture is applied to metals without change. Vibration of the lattice alone cannot explain why metals conduct heat so much better than non-metallic solids such as glass or wood, or why they conduct electricity at all. In a metal the delocalized electrons are mobile: they carry charge when a potential difference is applied and carry kinetic energy from hot regions to cold ones.
items.specStatementText: A metallic bond is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of cations and delocalized electrons.

items.q: When a metal is hammered flat, do the individual metal atoms change shape?
items.correct: No. The cations keep their size and shape; what changes is their arrangement. Layers of cations slide past one another and the non-directional attraction to the delocalized electrons holds them in their new positions.
items.misconception: A metal is malleable because its atoms are themselves soft and squash or flatten when it is hammered or rolled.
items.why: Students often attribute the bulk properties of a substance to its individual particles (soft materials made of 'soft' atoms, hot substances made of 'hot' or expanded atoms); this is widely reported in chemistry-education research on the particle model. Macroscopic properties arise from how particles are arranged and bonded, not from the particles having those properties. A metal changes shape because whole layers of cations move relative to one another while the metallic bonding holds them together.
items.specStatementText: A metallic bond is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of cations and delocalized electrons.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a metallic bond an attraction between cations and anions?
items.correct: No. A metal contains no anions. The negative charge is carried by delocalized electrons that belong to no particular atom; the metallic bond is the attraction between the lattice of cations and these electrons.
items.misconception: In a metal some atoms give electrons to others, forming cations and anions that attract each other as in an ionic compound.
items.why: Ionic bonding is taught as the model of 'electrostatic attraction', and 'the metal atom loses electrons' then seems to need a partner that gains them. Learners are widely reported to describe metallic bonding with ionic or covalent models. All the atoms in a pure metal are of the same element and have the same tendency to release electrons, so none of them forms an anion. The released electrons are delocalized over the whole lattice and attract all the cations.
items.specStatementText: A metallic bond is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of cations and delocalized electrons.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When a metal wire carries a current, do the moving electrons come only from the power supply?
items.correct: No. The charge carriers are the metal's own delocalized electrons, present throughout the wire. The power supply provides the potential difference that makes them drift; electrons enter at one end as others leave at the other.
items.misconception: The electrons that carry the current come from the cell or power supply and pass through the metal; the metal's own electrons stay where they are.
items.why: Everyday speech ('the battery supplies the electricity') presents the cell as the source of the moving charge. The belief that a cell supplies the charge that flows is one of the most widely reported misconceptions about electric circuits. A metal conducts because it already contains mobile charge: its delocalized electrons. The power supply does not provide the electrons; it provides the potential difference that makes the delocalized electrons already present drift around the circuit.
items.specStatementText: A metallic bond is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of cations and delocalized electrons.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When a metal object feels colder to the touch than a wooden one in the same room, is the metal at a lower temperature?
items.correct: No. After enough time in the same room both are at room temperature. The metal feels colder because it conducts energy away from the skin much faster, through its delocalized electrons.
items.misconception: Metals are naturally colder than other materials in the same surroundings, so they keep drawing heat out of warmer objects.
items.why: Touch senses the rate at which energy leaves the skin, not temperature, so a metal at room temperature feels cold. Taking this sensation as a reading of temperature is widely reported in research on students' ideas about heat and temperature. Objects left in the same surroundings reach the same temperature. A metal only transfers energy from a hotter object while it is colder than that object, and it does so quickly because its delocalized electrons carry energy rapidly through it.
items.specStatementText: A metallic bond is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of cations and delocalized electrons.

items.q: Is an electric current in a metal a flow of charge or a passing-on of energy?
items.correct: A flow of charge. In a metal the charge carriers are the delocalized electrons, which drift when a potential difference is applied.
items.misconception: An electric current is energy passed along the wire from particle to particle; no charged particles need to move through the metal.
items.why: Current and energy are routinely confused ("the current is used up", "electricity flows"). This conflation is widely reported in research on students' ideas about electric circuits. A current is a flow of charge; in a metal the charge carriers are the delocalized electrons, which drift when a potential difference is applied.
